Evaluation of forecast skill FitzRoy offers three main forecasting products: (i) hourly rain probability, (ii) instantaneous precipitation rate at the top of the hour, and (iii) hourly precipitation accumulation. We evaluate FitzRoy against physics-based and ML baselines on a strictly held-out test period comprising forecasts from August 2024 onwards, a period never seen during training or validation. We use MRMS ( NOAA National Severe Storms Laboratory, 2025 ) and in-situ station data from GHCN ( NOAA National Centers for Environmental Information, 2025 ) as reference. For hourly rain probability, we compare against three ensemble systems: the High Resolution Ensemble Forecast (HREF) ( Roberts et al., 2020 ) , the National Blend of Models (NBM) ( NOAA National Weather Service, 2025 ) from NOAA, and the ECMWF ensemble prediction system (ENS) ( ECMWF, 2012 ) . For precipitation rate, we evaluate against the control forecasts from ENS, the NOAA High-Resolution Rapid Refresh (HRRR) model ( Dowell et al., 2022 ) and the ML-based forecasts from StormCast ( Pathak et al., 2026b ) . For hourly accumulation, we use forecasts from HREF, NBM, ENS, and HRRR as benchmarks. In addition, we compare against the ML models AIFS-single from ECMWF ( Lang et al., 2024 ) , GraphCast ( Lam et al., 2023 ) , and GenCast ( Price et al., 2025 ) 2 2 2 For this comparison, GraphCast and GenCast are initialized using non-operational ERA5 reanalysis data. This introduces information that would be unavailable in a real-time operational environment. In contrast, the evaluated FitzRoy forecasts rely exclusively on operational data. Consequently, these evaluation results should be interpreted as an upper bound on the performance of GraphCast and GenCast rather than a direct operational comparison. . Since the latter three models do not provide hourly accumulations, we add up our hourly predictions to 6- and 12-hour accumulations for comparison. Due to the varying characteristics of the above baselines (forecast frequency, accumulation window, etc.) we present pairwise scorecards in Fig. 4 , where each scorecard evaluates FitzRoy within the intended scope of operation of the corresponding baseline. For each lead time, a cell in the scorecard shows the relative difference of FitzRoy compared to the corresponding baseline as well as the statistical significance following Hamill (1999) . We provide metrics definitions and further evaluation details in the supplementary materials. Across the evaluated deterministic and probabilistic precipitation tasks, FitzRoy is consistently competitive with or better than all baselines, although the magnitude of the improvement varies across models, metrics, thresholds, and lead times. The largest gains are observed relative to strong operational convection-allowing models such as HRRR and ENS-CF, as well as ML-based forecasting systems, including AIFS-single, GraphCast, and GenCast, which FitzRoy outperforms by substantial margins across most metrics. Against NBM, whose forecast is used as an input to the FitzRoy model, we similarly observe large gains across most metrics, demonstrating that FitzRoy adds substantial predictive skill beyond the forecast information it receives. Against the strong operational ensemble system HREF, the improvements are generally more modest, and some individual comparisons are statistically indistinguishable; nevertheless, FitzRoy consistently matches or exceeds HREF across the corresponding evaluation regimes. Similar behavior is observed for instantaneous precipitation rate and probabilistic forecasting, where FitzRoy remains competitive with or improves upon the corresponding operational baselines. To our knowledge, this is the first ML-based system to achieve this level of performance across both deterministic and probabilistic precipitation forecasting, effectively closing the historical performance gap between ML approaches and operational physics-based systems while exceeding existing ML baselines by considerably larger margins. We observe the most significant performance gains in forecasting rain intensities (Figs. 4 A and B). Relative to both deterministic and ensemble baselines, FitzRoy delivers superior discrimination between rainy and non-rainy events and substantially improved skill for heavy-precipitation thresholds. While operational probabilistic systems are often constrained by small ensemble sizes and the need for ad hoc dispersion inflation, FitzRoy’s uncertainty emerges naturally from its probabilistic components. This design yields sharper, more informative distributions that maintain calibration even in the tails. To evaluate the pure forecasting quality, we neglect here the data-delivery and model runtime latencies. However, in real-world operational environments, model latency is a critical bottleneck. We therefore provide a latency-aware evaluation in supplementary materials (Fig. S1), which adjusts the effective forecast lead time according to model initialization frequency, data availability, and runtime. Because FitzRoy can ingest recent observations and produce forecasts with sub-hour latency, this operationally aligned evaluation further increases its advantage over traditional numerical weather prediction systems, whose most recent available forecasts may already be several hours old at the time of use. 3 3 3 We also evaluate FitzRoy against MetNet-3 ( Andrychowicz et al., 2023 ) in the supplementary materials. Since neither source code nor operational forecasts for MetNet-3 are publicly available, we customize the evaluation protocol in an attempt to reproduce their reported results. To better understand the contribution of individual components to FitzRoy’s performance, we present analyses in the supplementary materials. Specifically, we study the contribution of NBM forecasts, the role of reinforcement learning, and key architectural and modeling choices. Evaluation of forecast realism Beyond aggregate skill scores, a precipitation model must provide faithful spatial structure to be meteorologically useful. We assess structural realism through power spectral density (PSD) analysis, calibration diagnostics, and qualitative analysis (Fig. 5 and supplementary materials). FitzRoy exhibits well-calibrated probabilistic and intensity forecasts across four intensity thresholds spanning light to heavy rain (Fig. 5 B). Forecast probabilities indicate no systematic over- or underconfidence. Intensity calibration, assessed via frequency bias, shows similar performance (Fig. 5 A): FitzRoy is unbiased for rain/no-rain events and yields event frequencies consistent with observations for light and heavy precipitation. In terms of spatial realism, FitzRoy closely matches the observed MRMS spectrum across spatial scales (Fig. 5 C), preserving variance from convective-scale features to mesoscale organization. Despite the tendency of ML models to produce overly smooth precipitation fields, FitzRoy preserves fine-scale structures evident in radar imagery and produces power spectra that are similar to, and at some scales even closer to observations than, the physics-based HRRR and HREF systems. These aggregate diagnostics translate into more realistic depictions of extreme weather phenomena. A qualitative analysis of 2024 Hurricane Milton (Fig. 5 D) demonstrates that FitzRoy captures the storm’s eye and spiral rainbands with high precision. While HRRR captures similar structures, its position errors grow at 12–18 hour lead times; conversely, HREF tends to blur these features. FitzRoy’s combination of accuracy and faithful representation of the fine-scale structure demonstrates that it can match, and in some cases even surpass, the realism of convection-allowing NWP systems. Case studies: forecasting catastrophic extremes To complement the quantitative analysis, we examine several high-impact events from the held-out test set and compare FitzRoy’s performance in a latency-aware setting against the baselines. Our analysis focuses on: (i) the flooding in the Texas Hill Country on 3–4 July 2025; (ii) Missouri rainstorm on 9–10 July 2026; (iii) Hurricane Milton on 9–10 October 2024; (iv) flooding in Connecticut and New York on 18–19 August 2024; (v) remnants of Tropical Storm Chantal on 6–7 July 2025; (vi) localized heavy rainfall in Ruidoso, New Mexico, on 8 July 2025; and (vii) the northern US derecho on 20–21 June 2025. These cases span diverse meteorological regimes, including tropical cyclones, organized convective systems, and quasi-stationary convection. In the main text, we highlight the Texas Hill Country event (Fig. 1 ) and flooding in Missouri (Fig. 2 ), both of which resulted in historic flooding. We evaluate Hurricane Milton (Fig. 5 ) as part of our realism evaluation and provide the remaining case studies in the supplementary materials. Fig. 1 compares FitzRoy forecasts with several operational NWP models for July 3–4 2025, when deadly and destructive flooding occurred in the Texas Hill Country. During this event, clusters of convective cells repeatedly formed near a mesoscale vortex and moved slowly over the same region, producing rainfall accumulations exceeding 300 mm in the early morning hours of July 4th ( Galarneau et al., 2026 ) . Public officials later cited limited information about the potential for such extreme precipitation as a contributing factor to challenges in warning and emergency response ( Gilbert and Yan, 2025 ) . For forecasts initialized at 18:00 UTC July 3rd, approximately 12 hours before the onset of the heaviest rain, the convection-allowing HRRR (Fig. 1 C, fourth column) substantially underpredicts the accumulated precipitation and fails to capture the full extent of the flood-producing swath. The HREF ensemble (Fig. 1 C, second column) indicates the possibility of localized heavy rainfall in central Texas, but its maxima are displaced and its spatial footprint too limited. In contrast, FitzRoy (Fig. 1 C, first column) accurately captures both the location and magnitude of the extreme accumulations, producing a coherent band of heavy precipitation aligned with the observed training convection and flood-producing region. Crucially, FitzRoy exhibits high run-to-run consistency. While the specific location of the heaviest rain shifts between initialization times in HREF and HRRR, FitzRoy’s signal remains anchored over the impacted region across multiple forecast cycles. This stability, combined with its ability to resolve mesoscale organization, illustrates how reinforced diffusion can provide actionable intelligence for high-impact events where traditional models struggle. For another high-impact flood in Missouri on 10 July 2026 ( Golden and Hall, 2026 ) , similar themes emerge (Fig. 2 ). A nearly stationary band of convection formed and produced extreme rainfall (over 200 mm in less than 12 h) and flooding in southeast Missouri. FitzRoy predicted a narrow band of heavy rainfall with intensity and structure similar to the observed storms, though with some errors in location. In contrast, other operational models underpredicted the rainfall, showed the band of convection in the wrong place, or both (Fig. 2 ). As with the Texas Hill Country forecasts, FitzRoy remains consistent with a forecast of extreme precipitation in Missouri while other models predicted smaller accumulations with more run-to-run variation. Discussion Precipitation is among the most difficult weather variables to predict due to its extreme spatio-temporal intermittency. Historically, a “skill-realism” trade-off has forced a choice between the structural fidelity of high-resolution physics-based models and the statistical accuracy of regression-based machine learning models. Our results show that this trade-off can be substantially reduced. FitzRoy achieves strong performance across 24-hour lead times while preserving the high-frequency spatial structure characteristic of observed precipitation. FitzRoy bridges this gap through reinforced diffusion. A precipitation tokenizer and conditional discrete diffusion anchor forecasts in physically plausible structures rather than the smoothed averages typical of regression-based ML models. Reinforcement learning biases the diffusion process toward high-skill trajectories, mitigating the “double penalty” problem, in which a realistic but slightly displaced storm is penalized more heavily than a blurred forecast. This allows FitzRoy to preserve the sharp gradients and high-frequency power spectra characteristic of real-world precipitation while achieving high accuracy in deterministic and probabilistic settings. A key strength of our framework is its flexibility across heterogeneous inputs. Using initializations constructed from physics-based model states and observations, FitzRoy already achieves strong performance. When an additional external forecast is available, its shared latent representation provides an effective mechanism for integrating this additional information, further improving forecast quality and allowing FitzRoy to function simultaneously as a forecasting model and a learned forecast-integration system. This flexibility makes FitzRoy difficult to place within a single conventional category such as autonomous forecasting, nowcasting, downscaling, or post-processing. Instead, FitzRoy spans these regimes, with its role determined by the information available at inference time. Case studies such as the 2025 Texas Hill Country floods and the 2026 Missouri floods underscore the real-world utility of our approach. Operational physics-based models, constrained by their reliance on idealized parameterizations of convection, failed to signal the magnitude of the event in time for effective emergency response. FitzRoy’s ability to resolve extreme convection with high run-to-run consistency represents a significant advance in forecasting high-impact, localized extremes. Furthermore, the computational efficiency of ML models addresses a critical bottleneck: the total time to forecast. FitzRoy’s low-latency inference provides actionable, high-fidelity forecasts in seconds, contrasting with the hours required to run a high-resolution physics-based ensemble. This effectively extends the actionable lead time for emergency management beyond what is currently possible with NWP alone. Ultimately, FitzRoy demonstrates that the synthesis of skill and realism is achievable with machine learning and leads to significant operational benefits. Reinforced diffusion and shared latent representation provide a blueprint for the next generation of operational meteorology. By respecting both the underlying data distribution and the fundamental dynamics of the atmosphere, we can move toward a future where weather events are anticipated with the precision and fidelity required for effective resource management and disaster resilience.
